teacher_glossary.definition: The law stating that energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between objects or transformed from one form to another. The total energy in a closed system remains constant. 'Wasted' energy is not lost; it is transferred to the environment, typically as heat or sound, and becomes unavailable for useful work.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students believe energy is 'used up' or 'disappears' during transformations — they think a light bulb 'consumes' energy rather than transforming electrical energy into light and heat, with the total remaining constant.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If energy is consumed, efficiency cannot be defined as a ratio (you cannot divide useful output by total input if some input 'vanishes'). Conservation is the law the entire standard applies — every efficiency calculation and Sankey diagram depends on total energy being conserved.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a system where energy appears to vanish (bouncing ball loses height each bounce). Ask: where did the energy go? Trace it to heat and sound. Then ask: is the total energy before the first bounce equal to the total energy after the last bounce? (Yes — if you include the heat and sound.) The accounting exercise makes conservation concrete.

sub_terms.definition: Energy moving from one object or location to another without changing form — e.g. heat flowing from a hot object to a cold one. The particle model (conduction, convection) and wave model (radiation) describe transfer mechanisms.

Energy changing from one form to another — e.g. electrical to light in a bulb, chemical to kinetic in muscles. In every transformation, total energy is conserved but some is transformed into less useful forms (typically heat).

Energy transferred to the environment in a form that is not useful for the intended purpose — typically heat and sound. Wasted energy is not destroyed (conservation still holds); it is dissipated into the surroundings and becomes unavailable for useful work.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think 'wasted' energy is a design flaw that better engineering could eliminate — they do not understand that some energy dissipation as heat is thermodynamically inevitable in any real energy transformation.
sub_terms.response: Ask: can you design a light bulb with zero heat output? (No — some electrical energy will always become heat.) Even an LED, the most efficient option, still wastes ~60% as heat. The 'even the best' framing reveals inevitability rather than poor design.

teacher_glossary.definition: The proportion of total energy input that is converted to useful output energy, calculated as: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (expressed as a fraction or percentage). No real system achieves 100% efficiency because some energy is always transferred as heat, sound or other non-useful forms. Efficiency is a measure of how well a system converts input energy into useful output — not a measure of total energy.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse efficiency with total output — they think a system that produces more output is more efficient, regardless of how much input it required. A 100W bulb is not more efficient than a 10W LED just because it produces more total light.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If efficiency equals output quantity, students cannot evaluate systems comparatively (the descriptor's 'analyse system efficiency' demand). A coal power station produces more electricity than a solar panel but is less efficient — the ratio, not the quantity, is the analytical tool.
teacher_glossary.response: Present two systems with different total outputs but different efficiencies (e.g. incandescent bulb: 100J in, 5J light, 95J heat = 5% vs LED: 10J in, 4J light, 6J heat = 40%). Ask: which produces more light? (Incandescent.) Which is more efficient? (LED.) Why? The comparison separates output quantity from output proportion.

sub_terms.definition: The energy a system converts into the form intended for its purpose — light from a lamp, motion from an engine, heat from a heater. All other energy outputs are 'wasted.'
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students misidentify which energy output is 'useful' — they count heat from a light bulb as useful because it can be felt, or count sound from a motor as useful because it is noticeable. The useful output depends on the system's PURPOSE, not on whether the output is detectable.
sub_terms.response: Ask: a light bulb produces light and heat. Which is useful? (Light — that's the purpose.) A heater produces heat and light (the glow). Which is useful NOW? (Heat — the purpose changed.) The same output can be useful or wasted depending on purpose.

sub_terms.definition: All the energy supplied to a system before any transformation — the denominator in the efficiency calculation. By conservation of energy, total input equals total output (useful + wasted).

teacher_glossary.definition: A flow diagram that represents energy inputs, useful outputs and wasted energy in a system, using arrow widths proportional to energy quantities. The input arrow on the left splits into a useful output arrow (continuing forward) and wasted energy arrows (branching off, typically downward). Sankey diagrams make conservation of energy visible — the total width of all output arrows equals the input arrow width.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students read arrow direction but not arrow width — they treat Sankey diagrams as qualitative flow charts rather than quantitative representations where width encodes energy amount. They identify where energy goes but not how much goes to each output.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The Sankey diagram's value is quantitative — it shows efficiency visually (useful arrow width ÷ input arrow width). Students who read it qualitatively cannot read efficiency from the diagram, cannot construct diagrams from data, and lose the tool's analytical power.
teacher_glossary.response: Give students a Sankey diagram and ask: what proportion of the input arrow width becomes useful output? Require them to measure or estimate widths. Then ask them to calculate efficiency from the widths. The width-reading exercise establishes the quantitative convention.

student_glossary.definition: Energy can never be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred from one place to another or transformed from one type to another. When energy seems to 'disappear' (like a ball bouncing lower each time), it has actually been transferred to the environment as heat and sound.
student_glossary.example: A bouncing ball loses height each bounce — but the energy hasn't vanished. It's been transferred to heat (the ball and floor warm up slightly) and sound (you hear the bounce). The total energy is the same; it's just spread out.

sub_terms.definition: Energy moving from one object to another — like heat flowing from a hot mug to your cold hands.
Energy changing type — like a battery's chemical energy becoming light energy in a torch.
sub_terms.example: When you turn on a light, electrical energy transforms into light energy and heat energy — the total stays the same.

sub_terms.definition: Energy that ends up as heat or sound instead of doing the useful job — it's not 'lost,' it's just no longer useful.
sub_terms.example: A car engine converts only about 25% of petrol's energy into motion — the other 75% becomes heat. That heat isn't destroyed; it's just wasted.

student_glossary.definition: How much of the energy you put into a system actually does the useful job — calculated as useful output ÷ total input. No real system is 100% efficient because some energy always ends up as heat or sound. Efficiency is about proportion, not total amount.
student_glossary.example: An LED bulb might be 40% efficient (40% of electrical energy becomes light, 60% becomes heat). An old incandescent bulb is only 5% efficient (95% becomes heat). The LED is more efficient even though an incandescent might produce more total light if given more power.

sub_terms.definition: The energy that does what the system is designed to do — light from a lamp, movement from a motor.
All the energy going into the system — by conservation of energy, this always equals useful output plus wasted energy.

student_glossary.definition: A special flow diagram where arrow width shows how much energy goes where. A thick arrow comes in from the left (total input), and it splits into arrows for useful output and wasted energy — the thicker the useful arrow compared to the input, the more efficient the system.
student_glossary.example: In a Sankey diagram for a light bulb, a wide input arrow splits into a thin useful-light arrow and a much wider heat arrow — you can see at a glance that most energy is wasted as heat.
